Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Avoid Religious Spaces: Places of worship or religious gatherings
issues.explanation: Avoiding religious spaces is not clearly linked to the indexed trauma of mugging/robbery, and no other selected Trigger, Memory, Threat, or Appraisal item provides a plausible religious cue or meaning that would explain this highly specific avoidance.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: The threat profile centers on generalized hypervigilance after robbery, but specifically listening for someone entering the home implies a home-intrusion context that is unsupported by the trauma type and by the rest of the selected items; this makes the item hard to reconcile with the same indexed event.

vignette: Layla, a 26-year-old non-binary veterinarian of Middle Eastern descent, has been struggling with the aftermath of a traumatic event. Three months ago, Layla was mugged in her own neighborhood while walking home from work late one night. The assailant had grabbed her from behind, pressed a knife to her throat, and demanded all her valuables. The smell of cheap cologne mingled with the metallic scent of fear that day, and she vividly remembers the way it clung to her memory ever since. Since then, Layla has found herself constantly scanning for danger, even inside her own home where she once felt safe. They had come to believe they could not rely on others for protection, which made them feel especially vulnerable. This sense of constant vigilance led Layla to engage in fawn responses when feeling threatened at work or with friends, becoming overly compliant and submissive out of fear. Layla's trauma was triggered without warning by everyday sights or smells that would suddenly remind them of the mugging. The smell of cologne from a client at the vet clinic could instantly transport Layla back to that night, leaving them feeling helpless and terrified once more. Unable to fully explain what happened when recounting the event, Layla often found themselves losing track of their thoughts mid-sentence. The constant fear and inability to trust others led Layla to adopt magical thinking as a coping mechanism. They would tell themselves that the event did not really happen or was not that bad, but these strategies only offered temporary relief from the overwhelming sense of dread they carried with them daily. This further fueled their feelings of isolation and misery. Layla's relationship suffered because they avoided going out together for fear of encountering a similar situation again. They began to avoid familiar scents and sounds in public spaces that could trigger intrusive memories, isolating themselves even more. The memories would often resurface when least expected, leading Layla to feel on edge constantly. One evening at the vet clinic, a strong cologne scent from another client triggered a full flashback of the mugging. Layla froze, feeling as if they were back in that dark alley, with the same fear and helplessness. The memory was so vivid that it left them shaking and unable to focus on their work for hours afterward. The trauma had fundamentally altered how Layla navigated daily life. They felt that going out meant exposing themselves to potential danger again, which led to more avoidance behaviors and reinforced their negative appraisals about safety and trust. This cycle of constant vigilance and intrusive memories made Layla feel as if the world was unsafe, leaving them in a perpetual state of fear. Layla's friends noticed the change but found it difficult to understand why they seemed so anxious all the time. The constant scanning for danger and fawn response at work began to affect their professional relationships and performance. What frightened Layla most was that these experiences had robbed them of the happiness they once felt, replacing it with a pervasive sense of dread. Despite the challenges, Layla finally sought help when the fear became too overwhelming to manage alone. They were most hopeful for finding ways to cope better and regain control over their life without feeling constantly on edge or relying on maladaptive strategies that only offered temporary relief from their trauma.
